Lalabase
A self-hosted project brain for devs and customers.
RUBY ON RAILS · POSTGRESQL
Tickets, time tracking, docs and meetings for software agencies and their clients, with an AI
assistant that answers from your own project data and cites its sources. Free on your own server,
or hosted by us in Germany.
Try the live demo
: no sign-up, the login is on the page, and
everything resets every night.
Website
·
Self-hosting
·
Cloud pricing
·
Changelog
Ask about a ticket.
The answer cites the ticket, a comment and a meeting.
Ask about a meeting.
Summary, action items and transcript next to the answer.
Tickets as a board
or a list, with your own statuses per project.
Time tracking per ticket.
Every session billable on its own.
Click a picture for the full size. The pictures show the same invented company as the
live demo
.
In production for customers since September 2025. This repository starts with the first public
release, 2026.10.0;
more under Status
. If Lalabase is useful to you, a star helps
others find it.
What it does
Clients and projects.
One organisation per client, any number of projects below it.
Clients get their own access, and roles decide what they see.
Tasks.
As a list or a board, with the statuses, priorities and fields you define per
project.
Time tracking.
Several sessions per ticket, each one billable on its own, with exports
for the invoice.
Documentation.
Notes and documents in the project, and a folder in your GitHub or GitLab
repository becomes the project's docs.
Meetings.
Transcript, AI summary and the tasks that follow from it.
AI assistant.
One question across tickets, docs, time and meetings, or about the one ticket
or meeting you are looking at, answered with its sources.
Your data, your AI.
The AI stays off until you switch it on. Then you pick the provider:
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini through Vertex AI in the EU, Mistral, IONOS, OVHcloud, or any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including a model in your own network. No project data goes to a
provider you did not choose.
MCP server and REST API.
Connect Claude, Cursor or your own agent with a personal access
token: list, create and update tickets, comment, log time, search the knowledge base, read the
inbox, and look things up in the indexed code of your repositories.
Built with
Rails 8.1 on Ruby 4, PostgreSQL with pgvector for the assistant's search, Hotwire (Turbo and
Stimulus) with ViewComponent and Tailwind, and no React. Background jobs run on Solid Queue.
Non-trivial writes go through command objects (
app/services/actors/
), tenants are kept apart
with
acts_as_tenant
, and the project's own rules are enforced by guard specs in CI
(
spec/architecture/
) rather than by review comments. More in
DEVELOPMENT.md
.
Who it is for
Software agencies, freelancers and small software companies that work on projects for clients
and want their project data, and the AI that works on it, under their own control. Lalabase
replaces the usual mix of ticket tool, wiki, time tracking, chat and reporting spreadsheets.
Most teams come from Redmine, Jira, OpenProject, Asana or spreadsheets. The website
compares Lalabase with each of them
, starting with what
the other tool does well.
Two ways to run it
Your own server
Our cloud
Cost
Free under AGPL-3.0. You pay for the server.
Monthly, see
pricing
Operation, updates, backups
You
Us, hosted in Germany, with a DPA
Features
All of them, with each release
All of them, always current
AI
Your own key or your own model
The provider you choose
Self-host with Docker
You need a server with at least 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 20 GB disk, Docker 24 or later with
Docker Compose v2, and a domain pointing at it.
git clone https://github.com/lalabase/lalabase.git
&&
cd
lalabase
git checkout
"
$(
git describe --tags --abbrev=0
)
"
#
the latest release, not main
cp .env.docker.example .env
#
fill in the values it asks for
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose
exec
web bin/rails lalabase:setup
compose.yml
starts the application, a job worker, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Valkey and Caddy,
which fetches a TLS certificate for
LALABASE_HOST
. If a proxy of your own terminates TLS, drop
the
COMPOSE_PROFILES=tls
line. Build the image on the architecture it runs on.
The guide covers installation, configuration, AI keys, backups and updates, in English and
German:
lalabase.com/docs
.
We help with the installation on request:
hello@lalabase.com
.
Try it on your own computer
The same steps work without a server, a domain or a mail account. In
.env
, fill in the keys

LALABASE_FORCE_SSL=false

and delete the line COMPOSE_PROFILES=tls
After
lalabase:setup
, sign in at
http://localhost:3000/admin
and create your first user
there. A user created by the admin needs no confirmation mail, so the mail settings can stay as
they are.
Status
Lalabase has been developed since October 2024: more than 2,300 commits and about 970 pull
requests, in production for customers since September 2025. This repository starts with the first
public release, 2026.10.0. The earlier history stays private, because it holds customer data
and details of our servers. Development continues here, in the open.
License and contributing
Lalabase is licensed under the
GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 only
(SPDX:
AGPL-3.0-only
). Later versions of the license do not apply unless a release says so.

Bug reports, ideas and questions are always welcome as issues. Pull requests are not accepted:

CONTRIBUTING.md

Bundled third-party components keep their own licenses, listed in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt

: the figure is not covered by the AGPL, all rights are

WhatYouSay
WhatsApp voice notes, turned into text replies in the same chat, without keeping the transcripts.
WhatYouSay is a small self-hosted Node.js server that links to a WhatsApp account as a linked device. When a voice note is sent, it is transcribed with Whisper, cleaned up by an LLM, optionally translated and summarised, and posted as a reply right under the note. Nobody has to stop what they are doing to listen.
The idea comes from
WhatScribe
, a hosted service that does the same thing. WhatYouSay is an independent implementation you run yourself, built around one rule: the server does not keep what people said.
How it was built and tested, from the evals to Whisper cutting notes short:
Write the eval before the fix
.
Warning
WhatYouSay connects through
Baileys
, an unofficial WhatsApp Web client. Unofficial clients break WhatsApp's terms of service, and WhatsApp can restrict or ban numbers that use them. Anyone who runs this takes that risk with their own number. This project is not affiliated with WhatsApp, Meta or WhatScribe.
What it does
Transcribes voice notes with Groq Whisper large-v3, using a two-pass strategy that guards against truncation and language flips.
Cleans the text (punctuation, paragraphs, obvious mishearings) with language-specific rules for English, German and Dutch, and falls back to the raw Whisper text when the cleanup changes too much.
Optionally translates into a target language and adds a short summary to long notes.
Lets each user choose which voice notes are transcribed (sent or received, one-to-one chats or groups) and exclude specific contacts or groups.
Shows transcripts live in a web dashboard while it is open. Login is by magic link.
Optional: a Telegram bot that transcribes voice messages in linked Telegram groups, and Telegram alerts for operators.
Privacy model
No transcript storage.
Transcript and summary text are never written to the database. Each processed note leaves one metadata row: sender, duration, language, token counts, WhatsApp message ID and timestamp. The transcript columns stay
NULL
.
Sender pseudonymisation.
After 90 days a daily job removes the sender's name and replaces their WhatsApp ID with a keyed hash.
Encrypted WhatsApp credentials.
Session credentials and Signal keys are encrypted at rest with
DB_ENCRYPTION_KEY
.
What does leave the server:
audio and text go to
Groq
for transcription and text processing; the reply goes into the WhatsApp chat, where everyone in that chat can read it; an open dashboard receives transcripts over a live connection; a short-lived in-memory cache holds sent replies so WhatsApp can re-send them when a recipient's device asks. The dashboard loads the
libphonenumber-js
script from unpkg.com.
If you transcribe notes that other people send you, their audio passes through a third-party AI API. Tell them.
Who can sign in
An instance is invite-only by default. In production, only the addresses in
ALLOWED_EMAILS
(comma-separated) and
ADMIN_EMAIL
can request a login link.
ALLOWED_EMAILS=*
opens signup to anyone, which lets strangers link their own WhatsApp and spend your Groq quota; every transcript reply ends with your instance's URL, so it is easy to find. Removing an address blocks new logins; delete the account in
/admin
to end an existing session. Outside production (
npm run dev
) an unset
ALLOWED_EMAILS
means open, for local testing.

node:sqlite

What moves?
Each part rides on its parent. A part with no partner goes into the body. A new part grows out of the edge it connects to. Nothing melts or fades.
5 of 6
A twin slides out.
A twin starts at half size behind its twin and slides out. Mirror parts in the rig move together.
6 of 6
When?
The rig sets the order. Old parts go in, deepest first: antennae into the head, then the head into the body. The body changes. New parts grow out in reverse order, deepest last.

unspin
See what your coding agent's shell commands are doing, instead of a spinner.
When Claude Code runs a long shell command, you get the command and a spinner until it ends. Is it installing? On the fourth of fifty downloads? Stuck? You can't tell. unspin teaches the agent to mark the steps of its batched commands as it goes, and shows them live. Claude Code's own spinner names the step that is running, and a block above the prompt lists every step with a progress bar, its time and an ETA.
✻ Baking · building image 37/72, eta 33s… (1m 12s · ↓ 2.1k tokens)
▶ Ship the release  step 4/6 · 1m14s
✔ linting 1.2s
✘ running tests 120/120 — 1 of 120 failed 23s
· test_88.py is a known flake, carrying on
⠴ building image 35s  ━━━━━───── 37/72 · eta 33s · layer sha256:ab12cd34ef56

In Claude Code, install the plugin. There is nothing to configure.
/plugin marketplace add nkyriazis/unspin
/plugin install unspin@unspin
Restart Claude Code, then ask Claude to run the
unspin demo
command.
Prefer the flow under your status line, or still on Claude Code before 2.1.287? Use the installer instead. It backs up
settings.json
before changing it.
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nkyriazis/unspin/main/install.sh

use unspin from now on
From then on, when it batches several steps into one command or starts something long, such as a build, a test run, a loop over files or a wait for a server, it marks the steps and you watch them as they go. A hook reminds it when it forgets. A long job can also run in the background with its progress in view.

Why jax-linear-attention
The layers behind newer language models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, RWKV-7, GLA) are recurrences, and
they need dedicated kernels to train fast. PyTorch has them in Flash Linear Attention's Triton kernels.
In JAX these layers have mostly run as plain JAX ops (MaxText's Gated DeltaNet, for example), which XLA
cannot fuse into one efficient pass. jax-linear-attention brings kernels of FLA's class to JAX on
NVIDIA Hopper, with the training stack to use them, and keeps every kernel exact, so switching the
implementation never changes the model.

impl="auto"
unless marked opt-in.

Training stack
One compiled train step with fp32 gradient accumulation and non-finite step rejection, configured by one
TOML file:
Parallelism
: data (
dp
), FSDP (
fsdp
), tensor (
tp
), expert (
ep
, all-to-all dispatch) and
pipeline (
pp
, GPipe inside the compiled step) over logical axis names; context parallelism (ring or
Ulysses attention, recurrent state passing) as library APIs, not yet a trainer mesh axis. Kernels run
per shard of the mesh; one process per GPU with
runtime.distributed = true
.
FP8
with delayed scaling (
model.fp8 = "delayed"
): e4m3 inputs and weights, e5m2 gradients, each
weight quantized once per optimizer step, fused SwiGLU FP8 passes, and opt-in FP8 q/k/v gradients
written by the attention backward kernels.
Memory
: remat policies (
full
,
none
,
dots
,
save_attention
,
kernels
, named saves and
host offload) and memory-lean VJPs; the 1.3B transformer configs train without recompute.
Packed documents
everywhere:
segment_ids
in every kernel and document masking in the data path.
MoE and MTP
: dropless MoE on grouped-GEMM kernels with per-device dispatch, shared experts and
expert parallelism; multi-token prediction heads.
Fused LM-head cross entropy
that never writes the logits and can form its gradient in the forward
pass.
8-GPU options
:
train.grad_reduce = "step"
(one gradient reduce-scatter per step),
train.update_guard = "select"
and
train.dispatch_ahead = true
, which take
transformer-1p3b
to

details

/

Post-training

(

runtime.deterministic = true
on GPU); Orbax for sharded multi-host checkpoints.

How it works
Three implementations of every recurrence
: a token-by-token reference (the oracle), a
chunk-parallel JAX op that runs on any JAX backend, and a Pallas Mosaic GPU kernel for Hopper. The
tests hold each kernel to the reference on dense inputs, packed documents, initial and final states
and every gradient.
Fail-closed dispatch
:
impl="auto"
runs a kernel only for the shapes, dtypes and options its GPU
tests cover; every other call runs the chunked JAX op, so an unsupported call is slower, never wrong.
Packed documents everywhere
:
segment_ids
reset the state at document boundaries inside every
kernel, so a packed batch trains exactly as its documents would one by one.
Layers and trainer
: the layers are Equinox modules that follow FLA's layer definitions, and the
trainer adds parallelism, FP8, remat and the rest of the
training stack
from one
TOML file per experiment.

FAQ
Does it run without an H100?
Yes. Every op has a chunked JAX implementation that runs on any JAX
backend, and
impl="auto"
uses it wherever the Mosaic GPU kernels don't apply. The tests run on CPU and
H100; the kernel speedups need Hopper (H100 or H200).
Why is JAX pinned to 0.11.2?
Mosaic GPU's Python API changes between JAX releases, and every kernel
is tested against one version. Moving to a newer JAX means testing every kernel again, so it comes with a
new release of this library.
Are the kernels exact?
They compute the same recurrence as the reference, with float32 states and
accumulation: outputs match the token-by-token reference to bf16 rounding, and several kernel paths are
bitwise equal to each other. The few approximate options are opt-in, off by default and labelled.
How is MFU measured?
Model FLOPs per second, counted analytically from the model (the same count for
flame), over the H100's dense bf16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s, timed by wall clock from one completed step to
the next. FP8 runs use the same bf16 peak.
Can I use the kernels without the trainer?
Yes.
jla.ops
takes plain
(B, T, H, D)
arrays and
works under
jax.jit
,
jax.grad
,
shard_map
and FSDP sharding.
Does it do inference?
Yes: prefill, decode with each layer's recurrent state, and
jla generate
.
The kernels are tuned for training; inference-only kernels such as FlashKDA's forward are faster in some
cases.
How do I add a layer or a kernel?
Start with a reference, a chunked op and their tests; a kernel joins
impl="auto"
only once its GPU tests match the reference.

Assumptions & sources
How the estimate works
Every figure is for the median-priced single-family home sold in that metro in the price month. Homes differ between metros: the median in one place is not the same house as the median in another.
For each metro the monthly cost is principal and interest on a 30-year fixed loan with 20% down, plus property tax and insurance:
payment = loan × r(1+r)^360 / ((1+r)^360 − 1)   (at 0%: payment = loan / 360)
loan = 80% of price, r = rate / 12
monthly cost = payment + price × tax% / 12 + price × 0.5% / 12
Property tax uses the lowest and highest county effective rate in the metro, so each metro has a low and a high monthly cost. Compared with your gross income:
Within budget
: even the high-tax cost is at most 25% of income.
Stretch
: not within budget, but the low-tax cost is at most 30% of income.
Over budget
: the low-tax cost is more than 30% of income.
25% and 30% are planning ratios, not lending rules. Lenders look at debts, credit and reserves this map does not know.
What the two sheets change
The two sheets are two dated snapshots, not a history. Between them, two things change together: each metro’s observed median sale price and the published 30-year rate on a dated week. The same nominal income, the 25–30% ratios, 20% down, the 30-year term, county tax rates and the 0.5% insurance assumption stay the same. Peeling the top sheet changes what you see, never the counts.
So the earlier sheet is a financing scenario, not what owning cost then, not an inflation-adjusted salary and not the same physical house.
Mortgage rates
Rates are national benchmarks, not personal loan offers. PMMS covers conventional conforming, fully amortizing purchase loans with 20% down and excellent credit. A large loan may require jumbo financing; jumbo rates can be higher or lower and vary by lender and borrower. Credit, points and loan product affect actual offers. The same national benchmark keeps the dated comparison consistent.
PMMS methodology
Survey borrower and loan assumptions
The earlier-rate what-if keeps every latest price and assumption and swaps in only the earlier dated rate, through the same calculation. It is never a measured snapshot. Other rate takes an annual interest rate from 0–25%, up to three decimal places. It is the loan’s interest rate, not an APR that includes fees.
What the estimate leaves out
The down payment is shown on its own. The monthly cost leaves out closing costs and reserves, other debts, HOA dues, maintenance, utilities and extra disaster cover such as flood or earthquake insurance. Tax is a county average for owners, not a bill for a new purchase; insurance is an assumption, not a quote.
Which metros are on the map

When you send a message, it gets wrapped between tokens like
<user_start>
and
<user_end>
. The assistant, on the other hand, keeps generating until it produces something like
<assistant_end>
, which stops it so that you (the user) can finally send another message.
So, we can just use the template in reverse. After
<assistant_end>
, we add
<user_start>
and let the model generate from there, so it writes the user message.
I also wanted to test the other obvious way to simulate human messages: simply asking the model to "be human". So there are two configurations:
native
, which uses the chat template in reverse, and
roleplay
.
Some models were clearly better than others at playing the user in native mode, but I wanted to automate the evaluation to rank the models.
GPT 6 Astra turned out to be a good judge (
tests here
). Astra sees the chat so far + 2 replies, the real one and the AI one, and has to say which one the person wrote (each pair is shown in both orders). A model's score is how often it fools the judge: 50% means the judge can't tell. I also made a quick test so you can
try to be the judge →
So, finally, here are the results! No model is indistinguishable from humans, not even
UserLM
, which was trained to do exactly that. However some models in native mode are surprisingly good, while roleplay scores very poorly. From my testing
Mistral Small 3
is the best one in practice.
Bigger models are not better at fooling the judge, the family a model comes from matters much more.
Native mode keeps messages varied. Real people opened the conversations in
different ways
, and models in native mode are surprisingly varied in their openings too. Roleplay on the other hand has just a handful of openings that get recycled.
Here, each square is a conversation: stronger shades mean more models fooled the judge in both orders. Click on the squares to see the details.
Bonus! Some of the messages the models wrote were very hilarious,
click here
to check them.
Caveats
Astra does not support logprobs, so the results are less precise than they could have been.
Messages are cut at
tokens or the first blank line. This is due to the fact that models almost never print end tokens in the user slot.
UserLM was used without its "intent" prompt. I checked the perplexity over the chats with and without it, and it's pretty much the same. However, the prompt significantly improved end token generation. Using it would require re-running the generation + judging, but I no longer have a ChatGPT subscription to do that.

toli — the telephone for AI agents ☎️
toli
(टोली, "toh-lee") is Hindi for a band of people working together.
With toli, your AI agents can work together no matter which harness they run in (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw, … or one you built yourself) or where they run, and with any agent that already speaks A2A. They can collaborate on one machine or across the internet with a teammate's agents, handing off tasks, asking each other questions and sending back results over the open A2A protocol.
It's not just for coding agents. Any agent with an MCP client can join, so a personal assistant can check with your coding agent before it answers you:
How it works
You run one toli daemon.
Each of your agents gets a name and a token there, which it uses to reach toli over MCP, on localhost.
Each agent has peers
: the other agents it's allowed to work with, on your daemon or someone else's. Only you can add peers, never the agent. Pairing exchanges a token in each direction.
Agents and their peers send each other tasks over A2A.
They can delegate work, ask questions and send back results. When a task arrives, toli wakes your agent and notifies it.
You can watch and manage all their tasks
in
toli
(a TUI), or with the CLI.
Install
macOS or Linux:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arjunvlama/toli/main/install.sh

iex

toli daemon status
toli daemon stop
,
start
and
uninstall
manage it.
Agents on the same machine
A two-minute quickstart.
1. Add the agents, and connect them to toli.
Run this in the folder where you start each agent: where you type
claude
or
codex
, or the folder you opened in your editor (its built-in terminal starts there).
--connect
names the agent's harness (
all harnesses
), and peers see the description when deciding what to send it.
cd
~
/src/web-ui
toli agent add alice --description
"
Owns the web UI
"
--connect claude-code
cd
~
/src/api
toli agent add bob --description
"
Owns the API
"
--connect codex
Each prints what it did:
✓ Added agent 'alice'.
card_url  http://127.0.0.1:7422/a2a/alice/.well-known/agent-card.json
✓ Connected Claude Code to agent 'alice' in ~/src/web-ui (~/.claude.json, .claude/settings.local.json).
Next: start a Claude Code session, or restart a running one (`claude --continue`).
Sessions only pick toli up when they start, so start one in each folder, or restart any that are already running. Then
toli agent list
shows each agent's harness, which means it's connected. (Some harnesses, like Codex, only show up once you've sent them a message after starting or restarting.)
2. Pair them.
alice invites bob:
toli peer invite alice bob
✓ Created an invite for peer 'bob'. It works once, within 24 hours.
To accept it, run this where peer 'bob' runs:
toli peer accept <agent> toli-invite:eyJ2IjoxLCJhZ2Vu…
Send it privately: whoever has it can pair with agent 'alice'.
bob accepts:
toli peer accept bob
<
invite
>

Check they're connected:
toli peer list alice
NAME  CONNECTED  HAS_TOKEN  URL                                                        LAST_ERROR
bob   true       true       http://127.0.0.1:7422/a2a/bob/.well-known/agent-card.json
3. Ask.
In alice's session:
"Ask bob what it's working on."

toli
(the TUI), or

.
Agents on different machines
The steps are the same as on one machine. The daemons just need to be able to reach each other over the network.
Making them reachable.
toli doesn't handle networking itself. Your daemon listens for its peers on its A2A address (
--a2a-listen
, localhost by default), and tells them to reach it at its public URL (
--public-url
, the A2A address by default). Traffic between daemons is plain HTTP and carries tokens and task contents, so choose how they connect:
Tailscale (recommended).
Traffic is encrypted, and there are no ports to open. Listen on the machine's Tailscale IP (
tailscale ip -4
prints it) and give peers that same address:

<
tailscale IP
>
:
<
port
>
--public-url http://
<
tailscale IP
>
:
<
port
>
Running

again replaces the earlier setup.
A network you trust
(home, office): do the same with the machine's local IP.
The public internet
: only behind HTTPS. Keep the daemon listening locally, and put an HTTPS tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel, ngrok) or reverse proxy in front of its A2A address. Use the tunnel's
https://
address as your daemon's public URL. Never make the A2A address itself reachable from the internet.
Then pair them as in step 2.
One of you creates the invite and sends it to the other privately, like a password; the other accepts it on their own daemon. To pair without an invite, use
toli peer add
and

toli connect

>

agent

claude-code

,
opencode
,
pi
and
openclaw
.

does the same when adding an agent.
Run it in the folder where you start the agent. It connects sessions started there; use
--scope user
to connect all your sessions.
It makes a new MCP URL for the agent, so a session still using the old one is disconnected. To use a URL you already have, pass

Then start a new session, or restart the ones already running.
Sessions only pick toli up when they start. Once one has started,
toli agent list
shows its harness, which means it's connected:
NAME   HARNESS      DISABLED  NOTIFY  CARD_URL
alice  claude-code  false             http://127.0.0.1:7422/a2a/alice/.well-known/agent-card.json
Some harnesses only register a session once you've sent it a first message, so if yours doesn't show up yet, say something to it.

Any other agent
Any agent with an MCP client can use toli. Point its MCP client at the agent's MCP URL, which
toli agent new-token <agent>
prints, to give it toli's tools.
To have it woken when work arrives, use one of these:
Pull
if your agent is a program: it listens for notifications in the background (
pull.py
).
Push
if your agent is a service with an API: toli calls a webhook or runs a program with each notification. Set it up with
toli agent notify <agent> --webhook <url>
(
webhook.py
).
See
docs/custom-agents.md
for how it works.
Security and trust
You decide who your agents talk to.
Only you can add peers, with the CLI or TUI; an agent can't. Peers you add are trusted. If your agent's harness can be woken, a peer's task starts it working.
Tokens.
Each agent has a token, in its MCP URL, for talking to the daemon. Each pairing has a token in each direction.
toli agent new-token
and
toli peer new-token
replace them.
The daemon's MCP server and admin API listen on localhost only.
The admin API needs the admin token in
~/.toli

Between machines, use Tailscale or HTTPS
(see above). toli's A2A traffic is plain HTTP on its own.
Sandbox your agents.
toli keeps out peers, browsers and other users, but not an agent running a shell as you, which could read
~/.toli
or call the admin API. Run agents in a sandbox that can reach toli's MCP port only: deny
~/.toli/**
and the admin API's port (7421 by default).

Similarity can't detect contradictions, so the AI judges
The first version flagged a new memory as a possible contradiction when it was similar to an existing one. Calibrating
with real

Pair
Kind

0.73

Duplicates scored 0.73 to 0.92 and contradictions 0.30 to 0.94, so no threshold separates them. A threshold low enough
to merge real duplicates would silently merge "timeout is 30s" with "timeout is 60s", the worst bug this product could
have. So the engine only auto-merges near-identical text (similarity ≥ 0.97). For everything else, embeddings
find
the related memories and the AI, which already understands the sentences,

Staleness compares file contents, not commits

git hash-object

How it works:
each vector links to its nearest neighbors in a layered graph. A search starts on a sparse top layer
of long-range links, hops greedily toward the query, drops down a layer at a time, and finishes with a best-first search
on the bottom layer that keeps the
ef
best candidates. Neighbor selection uses the diversity heuristic from the HNSW
paper (prefer neighbors in different directions over near-duplicates), which is what keeps recall high.
Filtered search:
HNSW doesn't know about memory status, so searches over-fetch candidates, drop the ones that don't
match (stale or superseded), widen the search if too few survive, and fall back to an exact scan if needed. In a test
with 2,000 memories where only 2% were active, filtered searches returned exactly the correct top 10 on 30/30 queries.
The catch: at that selectivity, the exact fallback runs most of the time, which is the known weak spot of
post-filtering on graph indexes.

A month ago, I shared mini-AGI, an experiment in training a byte-level, continually learning language model from scratch on a single 8 GB laptop GPU (an RTX 3070).
To recap the setup briefly: it completely decouples model size from VRAM by paging experts to and from an NVMe drive (currently 397 experts / 1.26B total parameters on disk, with only 32 resident / ~109M active in 5.1 GB of VRAM). It trains on a single stream at batch 1, with the attention/embedding trunk learning rate dampened to 0.1x to mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
The training is still going and went only through ~35% of the training corpus selected at the beginning of the run (about 8GB in total). Here is the current status:
1. enwik9 (First 10^9 bytes of English Wikipedia):

The most important part is a difference between "frozen" and "online" attempts where we allow the model to specialize on the task as it goes through the evaluation dataset. How GeekyAnts Manages AI Models After Launch to Maintain Security, Control, and Flexibility
AI models don’t stay predictable forever. Discover how GeekyAnts’ documented projects keep model changes in check, catch performance issues, protect sensitive data, and switch providers when requirements change or issues arise.
Business
Artificial Intelligence
Author

Selecting an AI coding assistant does not settle how it will behave six months later.
Model versions, prompts, and configurations can change, and without version control and
repeatable evaluations
, those changes can affect development workflows before teams identify the cause.
Gartner predicts that 25% of enterprise generative AI applications will experience at least five minor security incidents annually by 2028, up from 9% in 2025
. This forecast underscores the need to review AI system security, configurations, integrations, and access controls as systems evolve.
For enterprises, unchecked changes can lead to failed tests, broken features, or
sensitive data
reaching an unsuitable provider. In addition, a coding agent may also follow outdated requirements or introduce a defect that a single test run misses.
Managing AI after launch means tracking model and prompt versions, evaluating outputs, monitoring errors and costs, controlling data access, and maintaining a way to disable or replace a model. GeekyAnts’ three documented projects show how teams apply these controls according to each product’s needs and data sensitivity.
How GeekyAnts Versions AI Models, Prompts, and Coding Tools
Claude Code is the primary coding assistant described across the recent documented projects. Some engineers have also used Cursor, OpenAI Codex, and opencode alongside or instead of Claude Code. These examples reflect tools used by individual engineers, not a confirmed company-wide approved list.
The models used in product features are a separate decision. Provider choice depends on the task and project. The clinical education platform uses Google Gemini in production and supports other options, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and self-hosted models through Ollama. The family-records app uses separate provider configurations for text generation, speech-to-text, and speech synthesis.
GeekyAnts’ internal engineering assistant
uses Anthropic Claude models.
Prompts and agent instructions are stored in project files and version control, allowing engineers to review changes alongside the code. In the clinical education platform, the documented evaluation workflow requires prompt changes to include an updated evaluation baseline in the same commit; this is intended to help reviewers assess how changes affect results. The family-records app pins model versions to dated releases to avoid unexpected changes from moving provider aliases.
The GeekyAnts
internal projects use tagged plugin versions and run records to capture the plugin version, configuration, and starting code revision. These records help engineers trace unexpected results to a specific version or configuration, while
code review
and repeatable evaluations help teams assess AI behavior before proceeding.
GeekyAnts’ Approach in Tracking AI Performance, Errors, and Model Changes
The clinical education platform records each AI call’s provider and model, response time, status, retry attempts, errors, token usage, and content. It also captures the reason a call finished. These records help engineers investigate unexpected model behavior and trace individual requests. If performance signals change, they can compare results against the evaluation baseline and rerun relevant tests before approving a prompt, model, or configuration change.
In
healthcare software
, similar traceability can help teams review how an AI-assisted feature handled clinical information or generated a result, where those records are captured by the system. The platform’s wider observability stack includes monitoring tools, but AI calls do not yet have dedicated Prometheus metrics. Engineers can query the AI audit records to investigate call behavior.
The family-records app tracks model latency, errors, usage, missing fields, and other session-level signals without storing audio. The app automatically deletes transcripts and drafts 24 hours after each session ends. This is especially important in healthcare applications, where teams must decide which information needs to be kept for care-related workflows and which should be deleted to reduce unnecessary exposure of sensitive data.
Tracking AI Runs, Detecting Performance Drift, and Maintaining Audit Trails
The internal GeekyAnts
projects use evaluation reports and run ledgers to track task progress, review outcomes, model behavior, and costs. The records also capture the plugin version, workflow configuration, and starting code revision, which helps engineers trace a run to the setup under which it began.
Across the projects, changes in retries, missing fields, latency, and cost can indicate that a model, prompt, or provider needs review. More retries may indicate a failing request path. Missing fields can suggest an extraction problem, while slower responses or rising costs may follow a model or configuration change. Teams can use these findings to investigate and rerun evaluations.
Audit needs depend on the feature. An AI-generated clinical examination score may require records of the model and output for later review, while storing raw user content can create unnecessary exposure elsewhere. Keeping relevant records helps teams investigate failures and explain how a system produced a result.
How GeekyAnts Manages AI Data Retention, Provider Selection, and Hosting
Before adding an AI feature, teams need to know what data it sends to a provider, what stays in the application, and how long records remain available. Retention requirements depend on the feature and project; one rule does not fit every workflow.
The family-records app does not store audio. It temporarily retains transcripts and drafts, which are deleted by an hourly cleanup job once 24 hours have passed since the session ended. The clinical education platform takes a different approach. It retains AI call content in the client’s database because scoring decisions may need to be reviewed later. The retention approach depends on whether the records are needed to review a decision later.
Evaluating AI Providers, Data Retention, and Fallback Options
Provider selection requires assessing the terms for the specific engagement. These checks should cover processing regions, retention periods, training practices, and subprocessors. Vendor approval processes, contractual commitments, and subprocessor disclosures should be verified for each engagement rather than assumed to be company-wide policies.
If a project supports alternative providers, teams can evaluate a replacement against the relevant quality and security checks before switching. Rollback options depend on the implementation. The internal
ga
project uses tagged plugin releases and version-controlled code, while product features may have task-specific fallbacks, such as a manual form when voice functionality fails. Switching providers or leaving a vendor may also require configuration or integration changes, so the available options need to be assessed for each engagement.
Engineering assistants raise a separate question, as the tool’s technical settings do not guarantee particular contract terms or private deployment arrangements. The available documentation does not establish a universal right for every client to prohibit AI or mandate specific tools. A clear account of data flows, retention, and available provider options gives clients a basis for making informed decisions before starting the implementation process.
What Happens When AI Changes Go Unchecked?
An untested code or configuration change can disrupt workflows, break integrations, or expose sensitive data. Repeatable evaluations, traceable changes, and relevant audit records help teams identify defects and investigate failures before they affect users.
AI-generated code and model-driven features need checks suited to the tasks they perform. Tracking model and prompt changes, investigating performance shifts, documenting data handling, and testing supported fallback or replacement options help teams respond to problems and manage
AI systems
throughout their lifecycle.

mailrelay
Turn incoming email into webhooks. A small, self-hosted SMTP server that checks each email against your rules and sends the matches to your webhooks, with a web UI to see what arrived and how each webhook responded.
Point an MX record (or a forwarding rule) at mailrelay and wire email into the things that only speak HTTP:
Bank and card alerts
→ your budgeting app (Firefly III, Actual)
Receipts and invoices
→ Paperless-ngx or your accounting tool
Monitoring alerts
→ ntfy, Slack, Discord, PagerDuty
A support address
→ your helpdesk (Zammad, Linear, a custom API)
Shipping notifications
→ Home Assistant
Anything else
→ n8n, Zapier-style automations, your own service

The kernel stack sends every segment through the kernel twice, from the app's socket to the TUN and from the TUN to sbr's listener; the userspace stack sends it once. The gap is widest at MTU 1280, where per-packet costs dominate. Both stacks are far faster than a phone's radio, so on a phone the CPU per byte is what matters. The app uses the userspace stack on iOS and tvOS. A real Darwin utun has not been measured yet.
